name: Chapter 10: Biotechnology and its Applications
description: Tissue culture, GM crops, Bt cotton, RNAi, recombinant insulin, gene therapy, molecular diagnosis, transgenic animals and biopiracy

cards.definition: Therapeutics, diagnostics, GM crops, processed food, bioremediation, waste treatment, energy production

cards.text:
Three critical research areas of biotechnology: best {{c1::catalyst}} (improved organism or pure enzyme)
optimal {{c2::conditions}} through engineering
{{c3::downstream processing}} to purify the product.

cards.term: Three options to increase food production?
cards.definition: Agro-chemical based, organic, and genetically engineered crop-based agriculture

cards.term: Achievement and limit of the Green Revolution?
cards.definition: Tripled food supply, but not enough for the growing population; agrochemicals too costly for poor farmers
Any part of a plant taken out and grown in a test tube under sterile conditions
Capacity to generate a whole plant from any cell/explant

cards.term: Components of a plant tissue culture medium (Exercise 3)?
cards.definition: Carbon source (sucrose), inorganic salts, vitamins, amino acids, growth regulators (auxins, cytokinins)
Producing thousands of plants in a short time through tissue culture
Plants from tissue culture, genetically identical to the original plant
Many genetically identical plants quickly, all year round; e.g. tomato, banana, apple

cards.term: Which part is used for virus-free plants and why? (Exercise 1)
cards.definition: Meristem (apical and axillary): it is free of virus even in an infected plant

cards.term: Crops recovered virus-free by meristem culture?
cards.definition: Banana, sugarcane, potato
Naked plant cells after digesting the cell wall, surrounded by plasma membrane
Fusing protoplasts of two varieties with desirable characters to grow a somatic hybrid

cards.term: Example of somatic hybrid and its drawback?
cards.definition: Pomato (tomato + potato); lacked the desired combination for commercial use
Plants, bacteria, fungi and animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation
Vitamin A (β-carotene) enriched rice
Approved for commercial cultivation in the Philippines (2021), the first country to do so

cards.term: Industrial use of tailor-made GM plants?
cards.definition: Alternative resources: starches, fuels, pharmaceuticals
Bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis
Bt cotton, Bt corn, rice, tomato, potato, soyabean
Lepidopterans (tobacco budworm, armyworm), coleopterans (beetles), dipterans (flies, mosquitoes)

cards.term: Form of Bt toxin in the bacterium?
cards.definition: Protein crystals of inactive protoxin

cards.term: Why doesn’t Bt toxin kill the bacterium? (Exercise 4)
cards.definition: It is an inactive protoxin in the bacterium (option c)

cards.term: How is the Bt protoxin activated?
cards.definition: Alkaline pH of the insect gut solubilises crystals → active toxin

cards.term: How does active Bt toxin kill insects?
cards.definition: Binds midgut epithelial cells, creates pores → cell swelling and lysis → death
"Eat, Alkali, Activate, Pore, Pop": eaten protoxin → alkaline gut → active toxin → pores → lysis
cry genes; proteins are Cry proteins
cryIAc and cryIIAb: Cotton bollworms; cryIAb: Corn borer

cards.term: What are Cry proteins, who makes them and use? (Exercise 7)
cards.definition: Insecticidal proteins of Bacillus thuringiensis; genes put into crops (Bt cotton) as biopesticide

cards.term: Why are different cry genes used for different crops?
cards.definition: Most Bt toxins are insect-group specific; choice depends on crop and target pest
(a) destroyed by bollworms (b) fully mature boll
Meloidogyne incognita
Meloidogyne incognita (root-knot nematode)

Silencing of a specific mRNA by a complementary dsRNA that prevents its translation.
A cellular defence in all eukaryotes

cards.term: Natural sources of dsRNA for RNAi?
cards.definition: Viruses with RNA genomes, or transposons replicating via RNA

Nematode-specific genes introduced via Agrobacterium
make sense and antisense RNA
→ dsRNA
→ RNAi silences the nematode’s mRNA
(a) Control plant roots infested (b) transgenic roots protected 5 days after infection

cards.term: Why does sense + antisense RNA silence a gene? (intuition)
cards.definition: They pair into dsRNA, which the cell treats as an invader and uses as a guide to destroy matching mRNA

cards.term: Advantages vs disadvantages of GM crops (Exercise 6)?
cards.definition:
Pros: higher yield, pest resistance, less pesticide, nutrition
Cons: possible ecological harm, resistant pests, gene flow to weeds, allergy concerns, biopiracy/patents
Safe, effective, mass-produced; no unwanted immune responses unlike products from non-human sources
About 30 worldwide; 12 marketed in India

cards.term: Update: are there still only ~30 recombinant therapeutics?
cards.definition: No; hundreds of biopharmaceuticals (insulin analogues, antibodies, vaccines) are now approved; NCERT’s figure is dated

cards.term: Earlier source of insulin and its problem?
cards.definition: Pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs; caused allergy in some patients
Two short chains, A and B, linked by disulphide bridges
Pro-hormone with an extra C peptide, removed during maturation
Getting insulin assembled into mature form

cards.term: How did Eli Lilly make human insulin (1983)?
cards.definition:
Two DNA sequences for chains A and B put into E. coli plasmids.
Chains made separately, extracted and joined by disulphide bonds

cards.term: Why can’t insulin be taken orally?
cards.definition: It is a protein; digested by proteases in the gut
E. coli carrying human insulin A/B chain genes, producing human insulin
Methods to correct a diagnosed gene defect by inserting normal genes into a person’s cells/tissues
1990, a 4-year-old girl with ADA deficiency

cards.term: What is ADA and cause of its deficiency?
cards.definition: Adenosine deaminase, crucial for the immune system; deficiency due to deletion of the ADA gene
Bone marrow transplantation and enzyme replacement therapy; not completely curative
Patient’s lymphocytes cultured → functional ADA cDNA introduced via retroviral vector → returned to patient

cards.term: Why periodic infusions in ADA gene therapy?
cards.definition: Engineered lymphocytes are not immortal
Introduce the ADA gene into cells at early embryonic stages
CRISPR therapy Casgevy approved (2023) for sickle-cell disease and β-thalassaemia

cards.term: Why is conventional diagnosis not early?
cards.definition: Pathogen suspected only after symptoms, when its concentration is already high
rDNA technology, PCR, ELISA

cards.term: How does PCR detect low amounts of pathogen?
cards.definition: Amplifies the pathogen’s nucleic acid to detectable levels before symptoms
Detect HIV in suspected AIDS patients mutations in suspected cancer patients genetic disorders

cards.term: How does a radioactive probe detect a mutated gene?
cards.definition: Probe hybridises to its complementary DNA; clone with the mutated gene does not appear on autoradiography
Antigen–antibody interaction: detects pathogen antigens or antibodies made against it
Animals with DNA manipulated to possess and express an extra (foreign) gene
Mice (over 95%); also rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows, fish

Normal physiology: Insulin-like growth factor studies; Study of disease: Models for cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis, Alzheimer’s; Biological products: α-1-antitrypsin for emphysema; Rosie’s milk; Vaccine safety: Polio vaccine testing in mice; Chemical safety: Toxicity testing, faster results

cards.term: Human protein from transgenic animals to treat emphysema?
cards.definition: α-1-antitrypsin

cards.term: First transgenic cow and its product?
cards.definition: Rosie (1997): milk with human alpha-lactalbumin (2.4 g/L), more balanced for babies

cards.term: How could transgenic mice help polio vaccine testing?
cards.definition: Test vaccine safety and could replace monkeys

cards.term: Why are transgenic animals used in toxicity testing?
cards.definition: Carry genes making them more sensitive to toxins → quicker results

cards.term: Why are ethical standards needed for GM?
cards.definition: GM organisms can have unpredictable results in ecosystems; manipulation needs regulation

cards.term: Indian body regulating GM research and release?
cards.definition: GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee)
Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (renamed in 2010), under the Ministry of Environment
About 2,00,000; 27 documented Basmati varieties
In 1997 an American company got a US patent on Basmati derived from Indian farmers’ varieties crossed with semi-dwarf varieties

cards.term: Other Indian resources targeted for patents?
cards.definition: Traditional herbal medicines: turmeric, neem
Use of bio-resources by multinational companies/organisations without authorisation and without compensatory payment

Industrialised nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity.
Developing nations are rich in biodiversity and traditional knowledge
Second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill

cards.term: Can oil be removed from seeds using rDNA? (Exercise 10)
cards.definition: Silence/knock out genes for oil (fatty acid) synthesis e.g. by RNAi, so seeds store little oil

cards.term: Does our blood have proteases and nucleases? (Exercise 12)
cards.definition: Yes; that is why naked DNA/protein drugs are degraded and need protection
